title: YouTube
summary: Upload, transcode, store, CDN, and a recommendation path that often dwarfs the video path.
what: A video platform is two products: a write path (upload → transcode → object store → metadata) and a read path (watch page → signed CDN URL → adaptive bitrate). Thumbnails, comments, and recommendations are separate systems with their own SLOs.
why: It forces you to split metadata from blobs, to think in chunks not files, and to put a CDN in front of anything humans stream.
mental: A blob store with a transcoding farm and a phone book (metadata DB). The CDN is the product users actually touch.
points: Requirements: upload, process many renditions, watch with ABR, like/comment, search, recommendations. Availability over perfect consistency on counts.
Capacity: minutes of video/day × bitrate × copies. Storage dominates. Transcode is bursty CPU/GPU.
API: POST /upload (resumable), GET /watch, GET /manifest.mpd, signed GET on CDN.
Data: videos table (id, owner, duration, status), object keys per rendition, a graph for comments, a search index.
HLD: upload service → queue → transcoders → object storage; metadata DB; CDN; recommendation offline jobs.
Scale: chunked resumable upload, many transcode workers, CDN for 99% of bytes, shard metadata by video_id.
Failures: partial upload, transcode poison message, hot video (CDN + origin shield), region outage (multi-CDN).
steps: Client requests an upload session; server returns a resumable URL to object storage.
On complete, enqueue transcode. Workers emit 144p–4K plus a manifest.
Watch: app fetches metadata + manifest, player picks a bitrate, CDN serves chunks.
mistakes: Recommendations on the watch critical path without a fallback

interview.q: Why not store video in the database?
interview.a: Blobs are huge, sequential, and cacheable. DBs want small rows and transactions. Split metadata from objects.
Encode many renditions. A manifest lists chunk URLs. The player switches quality as bandwidth changes.

rows: Object storage, never the primary SQL
Queue + workers, not the upload request

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Putting video bytes in MySQL, or transcoding inside the upload HTTP request.

title: Netflix
summary: Open Connect, adaptive bitrate, and a control plane that is a microservice zoo.
what: A licensed-video streamer pushes bits to ISP-colocated caches (Open Connect) so the backbone is not the product. The control plane (catalog, auth, personalization, playback licenses) is many services; the data plane is files on appliances near users.
why: It is the textbook of 'move the bytes next to the eyeballs' and of isolating a noisy control plane from a boring data plane.
mental: A CDN you own, plus a website that tells the player which file to ask for.
points: Requirements: catalog, playback, resume, profiles, recommendations, DRM. Prime-time spike.
Capacity: simultaneous streams × bitrate. Peak is the design point.
API: auth, title metadata, playback license, manifest. The video URL is not your origin.
HLD: clients → playback service → Open Connect / CDN; control plane in the cloud.
Failures: appliance down (other OCAs, internet CDN fallback), license service down (no new plays, existing may continue), regional cloud (active-active control).
mistakes: Streaming from a single region origin at peak

interview.a: Last-mile and peering cost dominate. Pre-position popular titles; the backbone sees control traffic, not every stream.

rows: License service on the control plane

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Drawing one giant 'Netflix server' that both personalizes and streams 4K.

title: Twitter / X
summary: Fan-out on write vs read, a home timeline, and the celebrity problem.
what: A tweet is a small row. The hard part is the home timeline: for each follower, a tweet should appear near-real-time. Fan-out on write (push into each follower's cache) is fast to read and painful for celebrities. Fan-out on read (pull at view time) is the reverse. Production mixes both.
why: It is the canonical 'hot key / celebrity' design. If you only know one fan-out story, this is the one.
mental: A post is cheap. Telling a hundred million people about it is not.
points: Requirements: post, follow, home timeline, search, notifications. Low latency on home.
Capacity: write QPS is small vs timeline reads. Storage of tweets is fine; fan-out is the storm.
API: POST /tweets, GET /timeline, POST /follow.
Data: tweets (id, author, text, ts), follows graph, timeline cache (Redis list per user) for ordinary users.
HLD: mix — push to ordinary fans, pull celebrity tweets at read time and merge.
Failures: cache miss storm, celebrity tweet, search indexer lag (eventual is OK).
mistakes: A SQL JOIN of all followees on every home fetch
One Redis key for the whole site

interview.a: Write: push the tweet to each follower's timeline (fast read, write amplification). Read: assemble at view time (cheap write, slow/complex read). Hybrid for celebrities.

rows: Fan-out on write into Redis lists
Fan-out on read, merge at view
Async indexer, not the write path

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Fan-out on write for every account, including accounts with 100M followers.

title: Chat System
summary: One-to-one and group messages, presence, and delivery at the edge of consistency.
what: A chat system delivers small ordered messages with presence and optional groups. Online users want push (WebSocket / HTTP2). Offline users need a store-and-forward inbox. Group chat is fan-out with a membership list.
why: It combines connections, fan-out, ordering, and 'what does delivered mean'. WhatsApp-scale adds E2E encryption on top.
mental: A mailbox plus a live wire. If the wire is down, the mailbox still fills.
points: Requirements: 1:1, groups, delivery receipts, presence, media (via object storage), order per conversation.
API: WS messages; REST for history. Idempotency keys on send.
Data: conversations, members, messages (id, conv, sender, ts, body), device inbox.
HLD: gateway (sticky connections) → chat service → Kafka/queue → fan-out workers → recipient gateways or push.
Order: per-conversation sequence numbers. Causal across conversations is usually not required.
Failures: gateway crash (reconnect + catch-up), duplicate send (idempotency), split brain on presence (timeouts, not truth).
mistakes: Presence as a strong consistency problem

interview.q: How do you not lose a message if the recipient is offline?
interview.a: Persist first (or on a durable log), then attempt push. Receipts are a later write. Never only-in-memory.

rows: Fan-out to members, not a naive query
Object storage, message holds a URL

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: A single chat server with a global TCP connection table, or using DB polling every 300ms.

title: Uber
summary: Matching riders to drivers on a map, with dispatch that cannot be a naive query.
what: Ride sharing is a three-sided matching problem under a latency budget: a rider request, a set of nearby available drivers, a dispatch that must be fair and fast. Location updates at 1 Hz from millions of phones cannot all hit one database.
why: It is the geo + matching case study. If you only know CRUD, this design is how you learn spatial indexes and supply/demand.
mental: A map of moving supply. Hash the city into cells; only search nearby cells; lock a driver for a few seconds while the offer is out.
points: Requirements: request ride, match, track, complete, pay, ratings. Matching in a few seconds.
Capacity: location updates dominate writes. Use in-memory geo (Redis GEO, H3 cells) not a row per ping in OLTP.
API: POST /trips, WS for location and status.
Data: users, drivers (status), trips, payments. Location is ephemeral.
HLD: location service (cells), matching/dispatch, trip service, payments, notifications.
Dispatch: ring of hexes, filter by ETA, offer one driver, timeout, next. Avoid thundering herd.
Failures: no drivers (queue or expand radius), matcher crash (offers are leases), GPS lies (map matching).
mistakes: Storing every ping forever in the primary
Dispatching the same driver to two riders without a lease

interview.q: How do you find nearby drivers?
interview.a: Partition space (geohash/H3). Update drivers into cells. On request, query k rings of cells, rank by ETA, lease one.

rows: Stream locations for the active trip only

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: SELECT * FROM drivers WHERE distance < 5km ORDER BY distance on every request against Postgres.

title: Instagram
summary: Media upload, a follow graph, and a feed that is part cache, part ranking.
what: Photo/video social: upload media to object storage, write a post row, fan-out a feed (or rank at read time), serve images via CDN. The graph of follows is the same celebrity problem as Twitter, with heavier blobs.
why: Combines the feed problem with the blob problem. A good interview if they want both.
mental: Twitter’s fan-out plus YouTube’s transcoding, with a smaller video and a stronger CDN for images.
points: Upload: client → object storage (pre-signed), then POST metadata. Never proxy multi-MB through the app if you can avoid it.
Feed: hybrid fan-out. Ranked 'for you' is a separate candidate generator + ranker.
Images: many sizes at upload time; CDN. Cache-control is the API.

interview.a: The app server is a bad place for gigabits of photo bytes. The client writes to storage; the app writes metadata after.

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Uploading the photo as base64 in the JSON of POST /posts.

title: WhatsApp
summary: End-to-end encryption, a small server footprint, and queues as the product.
what: E2E chat: servers cannot read bodies. They store encrypted blobs addressed to a device, fan them out, and drop them after delivery. Presence and group membership are metadata; the Double Ratchet lives on clients.
why: It shows how little the server must do if clients are smart, and why 'the server is a queue' is a design, not a cop-out.
mental: A post office that cannot open the mail. Device keys, not user passwords, are the trust story.
points: Signal protocol: identity keys, prekeys, ratchets. Server holds prekey bundles.
Multi-device: each device has keys; sender encrypts per device or uses a sender key in groups.
Scale: Erlang-style cheap connections; store-and-forward only.
mistakes: One key for all of a user's devices without a plan

interview.q: What can the server still know?
interview.a: Metadata: who talked to whom, when, size, group membership — unless you go further (sealed sender). Not the body.

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Storing plaintext 'for spam detection' while claiming E2E.

title: Amazon
summary: A catalog, a cart, inventory, and a warehouse network. The original service-oriented giant.
what: E-commerce at scale is catalog search, cart, inventory reservation, checkout (idempotent payment + order), and fulfillment. Inventory is the consistency hot spot: two customers must not buy the last item.
why: It is the case for transactions where they matter (checkout) and caches where they don't (catalog).
mental: A warehouse plus a website. The website lies (cache); the warehouse cannot.
points: Catalog: denormalized search index, CDN for images, eventual on descriptions.
Cart: per-user, often cache + DB. Not inventory yet.
Checkout: reserve inventory (short TTL), capture payment, create order, release reserve on fail.
Idempotency keys on pay. Exactly-once is a ledger, not a hope.
mistakes: Holding inventory for abandoned carts forever

interview.a: Atomic reserve with a TTL at checkout, not at cart. Commit on pay success; expire otherwise. DB constraint or conditional write.

title: Google Search
summary: Crawl, index, rank, and serve in ~100ms. The original warehouse-scale computer.
what: Web search is a pipeline: crawl the graph, extract, shard an inverted index, retrieve candidates, rank (signals + ML), snippet. Serving is a fan-out to index shards with a tight tail-latency budget.
why: It is the IR + systems interview. Indexing is batch/stream; serving is a scatter-gather.
mental: A library catalog (inverted index) plus a very fast committee that votes on the ten best cards.
points: Crawler: politeness, canonical URLs, frontier priority, render for JS sites.
Index: term → postings (doc, tf, positions). Sharded by term or by doc; both exist.
Serve: query rewrite → retrieve from shards → merge → rank → cache the head.
Freshness vs cost: news needs a fast lane; the long tail can lag.
mistakes: Ranking only on TF-IDF in 2026 without saying it's a baseline

interview.a: Queries are terms; documents are many. Term → list of docs is the structure that makes intersection fast.

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: SELECT * FROM pages WHERE body LIKE '%query%' at 10k QPS.

title: Search Engine
summary: A complete IR pipeline you could sketch: crawler, indexer, query service, ranker.
what: Same bones as web search, scoped to a product: crawl or ingest, analyze, index (sparse + maybe dense), retrieve, rank, evaluate. Hybrid search fuses BM25 and vectors.
why: Most engineers will build this (site search, logs) long before they build Google.
mental: A write path that builds postings and embeddings; a read path that unions two candidate lists and ranks.
points: Ingest: events or a crawler. Idempotent doc ids.
Analyze: tokenize, stem/lemmatize, language.
Index: inverted + vector (HNSW). Refresh interval is a product knob.
Query: retrieve k1 sparse + k2 dense, RRF or a learned ranker, then snippets.
mistakes: Rebuilding the whole index on every document

interview.a: Keyword search nails exact tokens (IDs, names). Vectors nail paraphrase. Each misses what the other hits.

rows: RRF or cross-encoder on a shortlist

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Only vectors, then wondering why SKU codes and error IDs never match.

title: Notification System
summary: Fan-out to push, email, SMS, with preferences, retries, and quiet hours.
what: A notification platform takes an event, decides who should hear it and on which channel, respects preferences and rate limits, and delivers with retries. The event bus is the source; workers per channel are the sinks.
why: Almost every product grows one. It is a clean fan-out + preference + idempotency design.
mental: An event comes in. A rules engine says 'email Ada, push Alan, nobody at 3am'. Queues per channel do the rest.
points: API: POST /events or internal bus. Templates, not raw HTML from every service.
Preferences: per user, per type, per channel. Quiet hours. Unsubscribe is a legal path.
Idempotency: event_id so a retry does not triple-text.
Failures: provider 429 (backoff), bounce (suppress), poison template (dead letter).
mistakes: Notification in the request path of the user action

interview.a: In the channel worker, with jittered backoff and a max. The original product request should have already returned.

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Each microservice calling Twilio directly with no shared preference store.

title: Payment System
summary: Idempotent captures, ledgers, and exactly-once as a business requirement.
what: Payments are a ledger: authorize, capture, refund, payout. The processor (Stripe, a bank) is an unreliable network. Your system of record must be idempotent and reconcilable. Double-charge is a P0.
why: This is where 'at-least-once delivery' meets money. Interviews use it to test idempotency keys and state machines.
mental: A state machine per payment plus a double-entry ledger. Retries replay the same key, not a new charge.
points: API: POST /payments with Idempotency-Key. States: created → authorized → captured / failed / refunded.
Ledger: append-only entries, never update a row’s amount.
Webhooks from the processor are signed and also idempotent.
Reconciliation job vs processor reports. Humans for the rest.
mistakes: UPDATE balance SET x = x + 1 without a unique constraint on the intent

interview.q: A capture times out. What now?
interview.a: Do not retry as a new capture. Look up the idempotency key / processor intent; if unknown, a safe retrieve; if exists, adopt that state.

rows: Your ledger, not the provider dashboard

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Generating a new charge id on every retry because the first request timed out.

title: File Storage
summary: Metadata vs bytes, chunking, dedup, and a namespace that looks like a disk.
what: A Dropbox-like service presents a filesystem: names, folders, versions, sharing. Bytes live in chunked objects. Metadata (the tree) is a database. Sync clients upload only changed chunks.
why: It is the classic split of namespace from blob, plus conflict (two clients edit offline).
mental: A git for files the user did not ask to be git: content-addressed chunks, a tree of names, and a sync protocol.
points: Chunk files (CDC or fixed). Hash chunks; dedup across users if the product allows.
Metadata DB: nodes, versions, permissions. Not the bytes.
Sync: client sends hashes; server asks for missing chunks; notify peers.
Conflicts: last-writer-wins with a copy, or CRDTs for special docs.

interview.a: Edits and dedup. A small change uploads a small chunk. Identical files across users share bytes if you content-address.

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: One blob per file with no chunking, so a 1-byte edit re-uploads 2 GB.

title: Food Delivery
summary: Three-sided marketplace: diner, restaurant, courier — with ETAs that lie.
what: Food delivery adds a restaurant prep-time constraint to ride-sharing’s courier matching. You cannot pick a courier before the food has a ready time; you cannot wait so long the food is cold. ETAs are estimates with wide errors.
why: A matching problem with a perishable good. Good for talking about SLA vs marketplace dynamics.
mental: Three clocks: diner patience, kitchen, courier travel. Dispatch is a bet on all three.
points: Order: diner → restaurant accept → courier assign (maybe delayed until T-ready) → pick up → drop off.
Couriers: same geo cells as Uber, with batches (one courier, two nearby orders) as an optimization.
Failures: restaurant reject, courier cancel, no-show. Comp and re-dispatch.

interview.q: When do you assign the courier?
interview.a: Late enough that they are not idle at the restaurant, early enough that food does not wait. Often a few minutes before predicted ready.

rows: Geo match with a delay window

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: Assigning a courier at order time when the kitchen needs 40 minutes.

title: Ride Sharing
summary: Supply, demand, surge, and location at 1 Hz from millions of phones.
what: The product layer on top of dispatch: pricing (surge as a signal, not a punishment slide), pooling, and marketplace health (too few drivers, too many, in the wrong cells).
why: If Uber is matching, ride-sharing as a topic is the economics and the map.
mental: A control loop: measure idle drivers vs waiting riders per cell, change price and reposition incentives.
points: Surge: raise price in a cell to attract supply and damp demand. Communicate clearly.
Pooling: match two riders with compatible routes; extra constraint on the matcher.
Honesty: show ETAs as ranges; GPS lag is real.
mistakes: Hiding the price until after the match

interview.a: Supply cannot teleport. A city-wide multiplier sends drivers to the wrong neighborhood.

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: A global surge multiplier for a whole city when only the airport is busy.

title: Video Streaming
summary: Chunked files, manifests, ABR, and the CDN as the real product.
what: Streaming is not a single TCP file download. Encode renditions, cut into time chunks, publish a manifest (HLS/DASH), let the player pick. Put the chunks on a CDN. Live adds a few seconds of latency and a packaging pipeline.
why: The generic form of YouTube/Netflix without the social layer. Useful as a building block.
mental: A folder of 2-second files and a playlist. The player is a loop: pick, fetch, buffer, repeat.
points: VOD: transcode offline. Live: transcode in a pipeline, sliding manifest.
Keyframes at chunk boundaries so switches are clean.
Auth: signed URLs or cookies at the CDN edge.
mistakes: Chunks that are whole GOPs of 10 seconds on live (latency)

interview.a: A playlist of URIs to media segments. The player downloads the playlist, then the segments, and can switch playlists as bandwidth changes.

extra.title: Common trap
extra.text: One MP4 progressive download for a 2-hour 4K film to a phone on LTE.
